  content: |
      # Running bbhost
      
      ## What you need
      
      bbhost contains no game data. You bring:
      
      1. **The game files**: a dump of Bloodborne with the 1.09 update's files copied
         over it - the folder that contains `dvdroot_ps4`. Its
         `sce_sys/param.sfo` says `APP_VER 01.09`. The update can also stay in a
         folder of its own beside the game's, named after it with `-UPDATE` (or
         `-patch`) appended - `CUSA00900` and `CUSA00900-UPDATE`, the way shadPS4
         keeps a game library. bbhost then reads every file the update has from
         there and the rest from the game folder, as the console applies an update;
         the log names the folder (`FS update=`).
      2. **The 1.09 eboot**, decrypted to an ELF. Its SHA-256 must be
         `941f887a562aae054fac35af8cc8f27cf075f3d4cc2e029fb5ae2a663aaa5ae7`. Every
         patch, hook and engine layout in bbhost is an address in that build, so any
         other eboot stops at start with its hash and the version its dump reports.
         A dump without the update carries the 1.00 eboot, which will not do. When
         `paths.eboot` is not set, the game's own `eboot.bin` is used if it is
         decrypted already (a dump made for shadPS4), the update folder's first.
      
      Both must come from a copy of the game you own.
      
      And a PC with:
      
      - x86-64 Windows 10/11 or Linux
      - a GPU with a Vulkan 1.3 driver (recent NVIDIA, AMD or Intel; the Steam Deck works)
      - 16 GB of RAM and 8 GB of video memory are recommended; 6 GB NVIDIA cards
        play at 1080p too
      
      ## First run
      
      Started without a configuration, bbhost opens its setup window: pick the game
      folder and the eboot (both are checked as you go), choose the online server
      and account if you want to play online, and press Play. The window writes the
      per-user `bbhost.toml` and starts the game. `bbhost --setup` opens it again.
      
      Without a display (a headless run) bbhost writes a template config instead and
      tells you which paths to fill in.
      
      ## Configuration
      
      `bbhost.example.toml` lists every setting with its default. The configuration
      is read in layers, each overriding only the keys it sets:
      
      1. the per-user `bbhost.toml`: `%APPDATA%\bbhost` on Windows,
         `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/bbhost` or `~/.config/bbhost` on Linux
         (`BBHOST_CONFIG_DIR` replaces the folder);
      2. `bbhost.toml` in the working directory, or next to the executable;
      3. `--config <file>`;
      4. the command line: `--app0 <dir>`, `--data <dir>`, `--eboot <file>`, or the
         eboot as the last argument.
      
      The first log line names every file it read. Paths may use either slash; a
      relative path is taken from the folder of the file it is in.
      
      The in-game settings (F10, or the PC Settings, PC Graphics and Key Bindings
      entries the game's own System menu gains) are saved beside the per-user config
      in `bbhost-options.toml`.
      
      ## Saves
      
      Saves are in `<data>/saves/SPRJ0005`, where `<data>` defaults to
      `%LOCALAPPDATA%\bbhost\data` or `~/.local/share/bbhost/data`. Each time the
      game writes a save (at most every five minutes) a copy goes to
      `<data>/save-backups/`, and the newest eight are kept. To restore one, quit and
      copy its files over `<data>/saves/SPRJ0005`.
      
      The shader caches in `<data>/bbhost` (`translation-cache.bin`,
      `vulkan-pipeline-cache.bin`) belong to the shader translator that made them,
      which `shader-cache-build.txt` names. An update that leaves the translator
      alone keeps them, so it starts as fast as the build before it; one that
      changed the translator throws both away (`gpu: shader caches made by
      translator ..., this is translator ...: cleared`) and builds them again while
      the title and the loading screens are up, from `stage-manifest.bin`, the list
      of the game's shaders, which is kept. `BBHOST_KEEP_SHADER_CACHE=1` keeps them
      anyway. The files are safe to delete: the next start builds them again.
      
      ## Controls
      
      A controller works as on the console. Without one, the keyboard and mouse
      take over and the button prompts follow: the mouse turns the camera and works
      in the menus, and every action can be rebound (F10 or the game's Key Bindings
      menu) - to a key, any of five mouse buttons, or the wheel turned up or down
      (each notch a press). Hold Left Alt with the movement keys to walk, and two
      opposite keys held together cancel, both as in Dark Souls III. F9 opens the
      plugin menu and F10 bbhost's own settings.
      
      The mouse turns the camera the way Dark Souls III's PC version does: by an
      angle for each count the mouse reports, 0.25 degrees at the default
      sensitivity of 5 (0.1 at 0, 0.4 at 10), with no acceleration, no dead zone
      and no top speed, at any frame rate. The right stick turns it as on the
      console, and while the stick is moving the mouse waits. With a target locked
      on, a quick flick of the mouse switches targets. Mouse sensitivity and
      inverting either axis are on the game's PC Controls page; the game's own
      Camera settings are the stick's.
      
      With the mouse, the camera also stays where you put it: it does not turn by
      itself as the character moves - following the character round, or turning
      away from walls. Lock On with no target (Q) still swings it round behind the
      character. That follows the device you used last: pick up a controller and
      the game's own camera is back; touch the keyboard or mouse and it holds
      again. Mouse Auto-Rotation on the PC Camera page (F10: Mouse auto-rotation)
      turns it back on for the mouse too. It is the community's "Disable Camera
      Auto Rotation via Movement" patch made part of the camera - less its hold on
      the lock-on button's recentre; that patch, applied as before, still works as
      it always did, with any device.
      
      The character's name, a chalice glyph and the network password are typed in
      a box over the game, which stands in for the console's on-screen keyboard:
      Enter accepts, Escape cancels, Backspace deletes and Ctrl+V pastes. A
      controller's Cross (A) accepts and Circle (B) cancels. The boxes take what the
      console's keyboard offers - letters, digits and punctuation from plain ASCII -
      and a glyph takes its own 32 characters, lowercased as they are typed. The
      name box starts from `[player] name`, which the first key typed replaces;
      `[player] ime = "auto"` answers it with that name instead.
      
      ## Logs
      
      bbhost logs to standard error. The packages' `run-bbhost.bat` (Windows) and
      `run-bbhost.sh` (Linux) write each session's log to `logs/`. A bug report is
      most useful with that log attached.
      
      ## Troubleshooting
      
      **The eboot is refused.** It is not the 1.09 build. Use the update's
      `eboot.bin`, decrypted; the message says what the dump's `param.sfo` reports.
      
      **The game stops at start in `FileTransferTask.cpp(865)`, or the log says
      `patch: old-hunters skipped`.** The game folder holds files older than the
      1.09 update's: the update was never copied over it, or only its new files were
      (Windows' "Skip these files" when it asks about the ones already there). The
      log's `change appearance: off - not the 1.09 m21_00_00_00 layout` says the
      same. Copy the update's files over the game folder again, replacing the ones
      there, or keep the update in a `-UPDATE` folder beside it (above). Until The
      Old Hunters' own files are there, bbhost leaves the game as the edition
      without it: its title screen would otherwise be a flat green picture.
      
      **The graphics card stops responding.** When the GPU hangs and the system
      resets it, nothing can be drawn again in that session; bbhost stops the sound,
      says so in a box and exits. The next three starts run with the GPU's progress
      markers enabled, so the log of a second hang names the draw that hung - send
      that log. Overlays that hook Vulkan are a common cause: OBS's game capture is
      kept out automatically on AMD cards (`[video] obs_capture` changes that), and
      OBS's Window Capture records bbhost without any hook.
      
      **Wrong picture.** Wrong colours, a green or black screen, missing parts:
      press F12 in the game while it shows. bbhost writes that frame, every render
      target the last draws wrote and the draw list into a folder of its own beside
      the logs, `logs/f12-<date>-<time>/` (`build/` when there is no `logs/`
      folder, `BBHOST_CAPTURE_DIR` to choose), and the log names the folder. Zip it
      and send it with the log; `tools/f12_check.py <folder> <log>` checks it for
      the rendering bugs found so far. The images are PPM, which costs nothing to
      write; `BBHOST_F12_PNG=1` writes PNG instead, which any image viewer opens, a
      fifth of the size on disk, written over a few seconds in the background.
      `BBHOST_F12_TEXTURES=1` adds every texture the frame sampled, and the game
      pauses while it writes them.
      
      **Black or broken image in the world, or slow on a card with little video
      memory.** bbhost follows the driver's video memory budget as the game runs:
      it keeps the last 512 MiB for render targets, puts textures in system memory
      when the card is down to that, and moves them back once there is room. Every
      five seconds the log says `video memory: headroom ...`; look there, and for
      `video memory is full`, before anything else. Other programs holding video
      memory (browsers, OBS, a second game) shrink the budget. On a GPU with under
      7.5 GB free bbhost also holds less memory ahead (the log says `small video
      memory`). `BBHOST_VRAM_RESERVE_MB=0` goes back to placing everything until
      an allocation fails, `BBHOST_SMALL_VRAM=0` turns the small mode off.
      
      **AMD on Linux, no picture.** AMD's kernel driver only imports anonymous
      memory, so bbhost passes the game's memory to the GPU through `/dev/udmabuf`.
      If that device is not accessible to your user, the log says so; this udev rule
      fixes it:
      
      ```
      # /etc/udev/rules.d/70-udmabuf.rules
      KERNEL=="udmabuf", TAG+="uaccess"
      ```
      
      **AMD on Windows, slower in a window.** Play in fullscreen (Fullscreen in PC
      Settings, or Window mode in F10). In a window the desktop composites the
      picture, and AMD's driver then never completes the game's occlusion queries -
      the same as when the window is not focused - so the game, getting no answers,
      stops culling hidden geometry. On a Radeon 8060S at 1920x1080 that is 112 fps
      uncapped in a window against 161 in fullscreen, and at 60 fps the GPU 55% busy
      against 37%. The log's `occlusion:` line, every 300 flips, then says `0 dumps`
      or `left not ready (N queries unavailable)`.
      
      **Steam Deck.** Start bbhost from Steam (as a non-Steam game), in Game Mode or
      Desktop Mode; otherwise Steam's desktop controls send keys alongside the pad
      and every press acts twice. `tools/steamdeck/STEAMDECK.md` has the setup.
      
      ## Display and frame rate
      
      The picture keeps its aspect ratio, with ultrawide resolutions (21:9, 32:9)
      available in the settings. The resolution can be changed while playing.
      bbhost paces the game to the refresh rate of the display its window is on;
      `[video] vblank_hz` overrides a display that reports the wrong rate.
      
      The frame rate is the game's own speed, chosen when it starts (a change
      applies on the next run): 30 is the game as it shipped; 60, 90 and 120 run its
      logic at that rate; Uncapped steps it by the measured frame time (1/240 to 1/30
      s), at the display's refresh rate with V-Sync on and up to 240 fps with it off.
      Above 30 the game's step is the frame's measured time (at most 1/30 s), and the
      places that stepped a fixed 1/30 s a frame - physics, enemy AI, ragdolls,
      grass, the camera's easing, momentum, fades - follow it, so the game runs at
      the same speed at every rate (`engine/frame_rate.cpp`, from Kyo's FPS++ lists
      and yogesh1239's high-FPS fixes). The play time adds each frame's milliseconds
      with the fractions kept (the game drops them: its clock ran 4% slow at 60 and
      120). Above 60 and Uncapped the game paces itself
      and its frames are shown as they come, so 90 on a 60 Hz display shows 60 of
      them a second; a rate the machine cannot hold runs slower than real time in
      the few places that count frames.
      The follow camera runs the game's own values at every frame rate, converted
      to each frame's length, so above 30 it moves as it does at 30.
      `BBHOST_CAMERA_TUNING=fps++` runs Kyo's 60 FPS++ camera retune instead.
      `BBHOST_GAME_FPS=30|60|90|120|0` overrides the setting for a run (0 is
      uncapped), `BBHOST_UNCAPPED_FPS=N` sets the uncapped limit (30-240) whatever
      V-Sync says, and `BBHOST_FRAME_RATE_LOG=1` logs once a second the frame time the
      game steps by and values written from it. `BBHOST_TEST_FPS_SWING` (a test
      switch, at 60, 90, 120 or uncapped) moves the target while the game runs:
      `square:LO:HI:S` alternates LO and HI fps every S seconds, `random:LO:HI:S` picks
      a new rate in that range every S seconds, `jitter:LO:HI` every frame, and
      `sine:LO:HI:S` sweeps it - one process at two rates, or at one that never holds
      still, as a variable-refresh display or a busy scene makes it.
      `BBHOST_FIXED_TICK=<address>:<bytes>[,...]` (a test switch, same rates) runs
      a game function as a 30 Hz tick - once every other frame at 60, and so on, with
      the remainder carried - for logic that counts frames (`engine/frame_tick.h`). The start of the log says which rate
      runs and how many values and code sites were converted (`frame rate:` lines),
      and names any site whose bytes were not the expected ones (that rate is then
      refused: 90, 120 or uncapped falls back to 60).
      A frame goes to the screen as soon as the game has finished it; only its flip,
      which the game paces itself on, waits for the next tick of that clock. The game
      keeps two flips queued, and showing each frame at the tick that completed it
      held every frame two refreshes behind (`BBHOST_PRESENT_ON_ARRIVAL=0` brings that
      back, to compare). Every 300 flips the log's `pacing:` line says how late the
      clock's ticks woke and how long flips took from queued to shown and to
      completed.
      A flip completes - and what the frame used goes back to the game - only once
      the GPU has rendered that frame: on the console a flip is the GPU reaching it,
      and the game writes the next frames' data over what a completed frame read. A
      loading screen's flips, and those above 60 and Uncapped, do not wait for the
      clock, so they complete as soon as their frame has rendered; the log says how
      many of a loading screen's flips waited (`video: the loading screen's ...
      flips`). `BBHOST_FLIP_AFTER_GPU=0` completes a flip once the frame is recorded,
      as before: the game could then run several frames ahead of the GPU after a
      loading screen and overwrite what it had not read yet, which could hold the
      GPU for minutes.
      
      ## Online
      
      bbhost implements the PlayStation Network calls the game makes against a
      private server, so co-op, invasions, messages and bloodstains work between
      bbhost players. The setup window picks the server and links an account; see
      [online.md](online.md).
      
      ## The debug menu
      
      The developers' debug menu is still in the game, switched off. The **Debug
      Menu** plugin restores it (the community's "Restore Debug Menu" patch by
      Whitehawkx and auser1337): turn it on in the setup window's Plugins tab and
      start the game again. The `` ` `` key then opens and closes the menu (Key
      Bindings can move it). While it is open the character stands still; the arrows
      move, Enter opens an entry and Backspace goes back. Its text is in English; the
      plugin's **Menu text** setting brings back the developers' Japanese.
      
      The English is `plugins/debug_menu/strings_en.tsv`: each string's address in the
      1.09 eboot, a hash of the game's text there, and the English - no game text.
      `tools/debug_menu_strings.py list` shows the Japanese beside it from your own
      eboot, `missing` what has no English yet, and `check` tests every row (the
      hash, the printf conversions, the font). Corrections are welcome as pull
      requests. A few strings keep the developers' text because the game looks them
      up by name - the names the character scripts call the game's functions by, for
      one - and `check` refuses a row for any of them.
      
      The menu draws with a debug font the game does not ship. The plugin makes one
      from the public-domain X11 fonts k14 and 7x14, so nothing has to be
      downloaded. A `DbgFont14h.ccm` and `.tpf` of your own in the mods folder
      (`<mods>/dvdroot_ps4/adhoc/font/`; [modding.md](modding.md)) are used instead -
      `tools/build_debug_assets.sh` puts the community "Debug Menu Restoration"
      package's original font there.
      
      **Playing online:** the menu can hand out items and change the rules, so
      sessions with the plugin on keep their messages, bloodstains and statistics
      apart from other players'. Using it to cheat against other players - in their
      worlds, in invasions or on the leaderboards - gets an account banned. Trying it
      out online with friends is fine.

=== kernel commit ===
commit 5773be0003eb50f81b5044c6f15fb85802862248
Author: realcryptopepe <184545674+cryptopepy@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Wed Oct 14 18:28:08 2026 -0600

    kernel: BB_DMEM_MB names the direct memory pool
    
    The direct memory the game is told it has is the stock 6 GiB, grown for a
    scene above 1080p through the GFX heap path. BB_DMEM_MB now names another pool
    size in MiB, clamped to the 7.75 GiB window reserved for it.

diff --git a/src/hle/kernel.cpp b/src/hle/kernel.cpp
index 8c2e25d..212d2c1 100755
--- a/src/hle/kernel.cpp
+++ b/src/hle/kernel.cpp
@@ -55,7 +55,17 @@ std::mutex g_dmem_mu;
 // window reserved for it holds - it ends below the image's fallback base.
 constexpr std::uint64_t kDmemBaseSize = 0x180000000ull;
 constexpr std::uint64_t kDmemMaxSize = 0x1f0000000ull;
-std::uint64_t g_dmem_size = kDmemBaseSize;  // fixed once the backing exists
+// bbport (BB_DMEM_MB): the direct memory the game is told it has, in MiB. The
+// stock 6 GiB (kDmemBaseSize); BB_DMEM_MB names another (the port's larger pool
+// for a scene above 1080p is 9152 MiB), clamped to what the window reserved for
+// it holds (kDmemMaxSize, 7.75 GiB). Fixed once the backing exists.
+std::uint64_t g_dmem_size = [] {
+    const char* e = std::getenv("BB_DMEM_MB");
+    if (!e || !*e) return kDmemBaseSize;
+    const std::uint64_t mib = std::strtoull(e, nullptr, 10);
+    if (!mib) return kDmemBaseSize;
+    return std::min(kDmemMaxSize, std::max<std::uint64_t>(512ull << 20, mib << 20));
+}();
 // Gnm addresses are 40-bit. Place CPU dmem below 2^40 so (va >> 8) << 8 is identity.
 constexpr std::uint64_t kDmemVaBase = 0x100000000ull;
 // GX also fills command buffers at this window + phys when phys fits in 4 GiB.

> 
> Now the "issues that stand out before compiling". Let me carefully review the evict logic for a logic bug:
> 
> ```
> const bool at_reserve = vram_within_reserve(kWant);
> const bool pressured = budget && used_pct >= pressure_pct;
> if (!at_reserve && !pressured) return;
> if (free_in_blocks >= kWant && !pressured) return;
> const std::uint64_t target = free_in_blocks >= kWant ? kWant : kWant - free_in_blocks;
> ```
> 
> When pressured and free_in_blocks >= kWant, target = kWant (evict 256MB worth). When not pressured but at_reserve and free_in_blocks < kWant, target = kWant - free_in_blocks. OK. Reasonable.
> 
> But a subtle issue: the original returned early if `!vram_within_reserve(kWant)`. Now `pressured` can trigger sweeping when the driver budget is 85% used but bbhost still has lots of headroom. That's the intent (port behavior). Fine.
> 
> Another concern: the sweep's condition `if (!sf.used_ms || now - sf.used_ms < idle_ms) continue;` — with the new used_flip guard, a surface used recently in flips is skipped. Fine.
> 
> However there's a potential issue: `surface_in_recent_use` computes `std::max(gc_recent_frames(), image_free_delay_frames())` on every call and reads `hle_video_flip_count()`. Fine.
> 
> In `textures_retire_reused_locked`, our guard is placed before the checks and uses `++it; continue;` — correct.
> 
> Wait — one important detail: in the retire function, `surface_in_recent_use` skipping means a retired/reused surface may never be retired... but it's a guard for safety, acceptable.

> 1. **`vram_budget_bytes()` semantics vs `vram_headroom()` — a real mismatch.** `g.local_budget` is the budget of the local heap, but `vram_headroom()` prefers `bb_memory_test_limited()` (BBHOST_TEST_VRAM_MB / test path) and, more importantly, when `g.has_memory_budget` it reads `mb.heapBudget[g.local_heap] - mb.heapUsage[g.local_heap]` — the *live driver* budget/usage, which is not the same as `g.local_budget` (the value captured at startup). So `used = budget - headroom` computed from the startup `g.local_budget` mixes a startup budget with a live headroom. Hmm — headroom is (live budget - live usage), and our used = local_budget - headroom. So used_pct = (local_budget - (liveBudget - liveUsage))/local_budget. If the driver's live budget drifts, this can be wrong, possibly negative → underflow. headroom can exceed local_budget if liveBudget grows. Then `used = budget - min(budget, head)` where head>budget → min = budget → used = 0 → 0%. OK, no underflow because of std::min clamp. Good. But it's semantically inaccurate. Also `bb_memory_test_limited` path (BBHOST_TEST_VRAM_MB) — headroom from the test limit while budget from g.local_budget which was also min'd with test bytes. Actually g.local_budget = min(heap/budget, test_bytes), and test_limited returns limit - used where limit is probably test bytes. So used = test_bytes - (test - testused) = testused. Consistent-ish.

Actually the headroom already returns negative when over budget in some paths. Let me reconsider: bbhost's own reserve trigger uses headroom < reserve. VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryBudgetProperties heapUsage = "the current usage of the heap by the process"? Actually according to spec, heapUsage is "the current usage of the heap, in bytes, by the process"... hmm, it's the amount of memory used by the heap — I believe it's process-wide usage. And heapBudget = "the budget of the heap available to the process". So headroom = budget_available - used_by_process. local_budget at startup = heapBudget - heapUsage at startup (they computed `mb.heapBudget - min(heapBudget, heapUsage)`) = free-for-us at startup. So mixing: used = (free at startup) - (free now) → the growth in usage. That's actually exactly `local - local_at_startup`, which is close to what they want (how much *we* added). But if other programs (browser) start and reduce our budget, used increases though it's not ours. Minor imprecision; acceptable and arguably conservative (sweeps earlier). I'll mention it as a note, not a blocker. Actually the cleaner statement: `used` should be `bb_memory_local_bytes()` (our mirrored/local allocations) and `budget` `g.local_budget`. > _Reasoning_
> Confirmed: `host_thread_set_class` is a no-op on Linux (`#else (void)on; ...`). This is the "GPU thread priority / audio thread priority" item from the Windows port, and on Linux it does nothing. That's a concrete, easy, low-risk perf item: implement the Linux branch using `pthread_setschedparam` (SCHED_OTHER with nice, or SCHED_FIFO/RR requires privileges; safest: set nice value via `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, -5)` — but that needs CAP_SYS_NICE unless RLIMIT_NICE allows; can use `pthread_setschedparam` SCHED_OTHER with sched_priority 0 → not useful. Realistically: `nice()`/`setpriority` for the calling thread with `-nice` may fail with EPERM. Alternative: `pthread_setschedparam(SCHED_FIFO)` fails without privileges. So the practical Linux approach is setpriority and log the result. That's still a legit easy improvement, though it may be a no-op without privileges. Worth flagging as "gated, log whether it worked".
> 
> Hmm, but the deployed `nice` trick: Linux `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, tid, -5)` requires CAP_SYS_NICE. Without it, fails. Could use `sched_setscheduler` with `SCHED_BATCH`? Not helpful. Honestly the reliably-useful Linux knob is I/O? No. There is also `SCHED_OTHER` + `thread nice` only. Or use `pthread_setschedparam` after `pthread_setschedprio`. All need privileges.
> 
> Better Linux-appropriate technique: use `sched_setattr` with `SCHED_DEADLINE`? No.
> 
> Actually there's `RLIMIT_NICE`: a process can lower its nice to 20 - rlimit. Typically rlimit_nice soft = 0 → may set nice down to 0 only. Setting negative nice requires CAP_SYS_NICE. So without privileges, cannot raise priority on Linux. That's why it's a no-op. So flagging it is legitimate but the fix is "try and log; needs privilege or a realtime scheduling policy".
> 
> Alternatively: a more portable Linux win from the Windows list is `BB_PRECISE_PACING` — bbhost already has pacing (`pacing:` line).

> For (B), the issues that stand out:
> 1. **`vram_budget_bytes()` returns a startup snapshot (`g.local_budget`) while `vram_headroom()` returns a live `heapBudget - heapUsage`.** Our `used = budget - headroom` can therefore be wrong (and is affected by other programs). If another process grabs VRAM, the sweep fires earlier — arguably fine, but the doc comment claims budget is "the driver's budget for the heap", which is only true at startup. A cheap, exact alternative: use `bb_memory_local_bytes()` for `used` (the same measure vram_headroom's fallback uses) — or expose a `vram_used_bytes()`. Also `bb_memory_test_limited` (BBHOST_TEST_VRAM_MB) path bypasses both, so pressure behaves differently under test.
> 
> Actually wait — more carefully: is headroom wrong? `vram_headroom()` = live heapBudget - live heapUsage. When has_memory_budget. And g.local_budget = heap budget - usage at startup. So `budget - headroom` = (B0-U0) - (B1-U1) = growth. Under the same driver budget B0=B1, this equals U1-U0 = our growth plus others'. Fine-ish. But `used_pct` then is "growth as % of free-at-start", not "share of the budget used". The port says "Above 85% of the driver's VRAM budget". Here we compute % of the free-at-start bytes, so with a 16 GB card it'd be 85% of ~15 GB free → ~13 GB growth, similar. Not exact but the direction is right. I'll flag as "semantics differ from the Windows doc; consider measuring used = bb_memory_local_bytes() against heap size".
> 
> Hmm, actually simpler and most faithful: `used = budget - headroom` where budget should be live budget. We could just compute pressure directly from what vram_headroom already gives: pressure when headroom < (1 - pct) * budget. That's exactly equivalent to used_pct >= pct when budget is live. Since headroom is the live free amount and budget a proxy for capacity, `headroom < (100-pct)% * budget` ≈ same. Both are proxies. Fine. I'll note it as a minor semantic caveat, not a bug.
> 
> 2. **The eviction gate is now inside a function that runs at most once per second (`now - last_ms < 1000`), and the pressure path keeps `at_reserve` semantics. Looks OK.
> 
> 3. **A real logic risk**: `static const unsigned pressure_pct = ...` and `static const bool evict_off` read `BBHOST_VRAM_EVICT_S` twice; `evict_off` is only true when the value is exactly "0". > _Reasoning_
> Important: `hle_kernel_set_dmem_size` clamps to `[kDmemBaseSize, kDmemMaxSize]` — i.e. minimum 6 GiB. But our `BB_DMEM_MB` initializer allows going *below* 6 GiB (min 512 MiB), setting g_dmem_size = e.g. 4096 MiB. That's a behavioral asymmetry: BB_DMEM_MB can shrink below the stock 6 GiB, but `hle_kernel_set_dmem_size` will clamp any later grow call back up to at least 6 GiB. Is shrinking below stock safe? The game expects at least 6 GiB; making it smaller could crash the game! The Windows port only ever *increases* (9152 vs 5056). Allowing BB_DMEM_MB to *reduce* the pool below the stock size is a footgun — a user setting `BB_DMEM_MB=4096` would tell the game it has less direct memory than the console's stock, likely crashing. That's a genuine issue worth flagging: clamp the lower bound to `kDmemBaseSize` (the stock 6 GiB), consistent with `hle_kernel_set_dmem_size`.

          const std::uint64_t slide = g_known_slide.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
          constexpr std::uint64_t kPoolHolderElf = 0x54b8788;

So `used = budget - headroom` is "growth since start", not "share of budget used", and other programs taking VRAM moves it. Continued. The BB_DMEM_MB footgun is fixed and committed, plus the doc corrections. Here's the review.

## Fixed now (committed on `awakechan-fixes`, no attribution)

- **`81ed11c` — `BB_DMEM_MB` could *shrink* the pool.** My port floored it at 512 MiB, but bbhost's own `hle_kernel_set_dmem_size()` (`hle/kernel.cpp:625`) clamps to `[kDmemBaseSize, kDmemMaxSize]` = 6–7.75 GiB precisely because the game's heaps don't fit below stock. `BB_DMEM_MB=4096` would have told the game it had less direct memory than the console. Now clamped to the same window (also kills a shift overflow on absurd input).
- **`e685767` — FIXES-LOG corrections.** The eviction idle is 30 s where bbhost's was 20 s (not "20 s kept"); the hang guard's two frame counts share one floor, so setting one alone to 0 doesn't switch it off; `BB_DMEM_MB` only raises the pool.

## Still standing in the ported code (won't fail the build, know them before you judge behavior)

- **`vram_budget_bytes()` isn't the budget `vram_headroom()` uses.** It returns `g.local_budget` captured at device creation (`gpu.cpp:2232`), while the pressure math pairs it with the *live* `heapBudget − heapUsage` (`gpu.cpp:4536`). So `used = budget − headroom` measures growth since start, not share-of-budget used, and another program taking VRAM moves it (sweeps earlier — conservative, not wrong). The log/comment wording is stronger than the measurement.
- **`BBHOST_TEST_VRAM_MB` bypasses it**: `vram_headroom()` prefers `bb_memory_test_limited()`, so the new 85% trigger never fires in that test mode while the reserve trigger does.
- **A single `=0` doesn't turn the hang guard off** — `max(48, 0)` is still 48. Only both zero disables it. Now documented.

Compile-risk check by eye: `hle_video_flip_count()` comes from `hle/modules.h` (already included by `textures.cpp`), `<algorithm>` is in both files, `vram_budget_bytes()` matches its declaration. I don't see anything that should fail clang.

## Windows docs, another pass

Your engine README's table is ~60 rows; ~50 are bbport/shadPS4- or Windows-only (MSYS2 build, PGO, DirectSound, Intel redzone patches, bbbridge, Xbox icons, launcher). Of the rest:

- **Linux thread priority is a no-op.** `host_thread_set_class` (`core/host_clock.cpp:158`) is Windows-only — 5 GPU-side threads call it (`gpu.cpp:173`, `recorder.cpp:582`, `gnm_exec.cpp:2206`, `window.cpp:2153`, `video.cpp:559`) and on Linux it does nothing. This is the port's `BB_GPU_THREAD_PRIORITY`/`BB_AUDIO_THREAD_PRIORITY` with no Linux counterpart. Easy to add, but honest caveat: raising priority needs privileges (negative nice needs CAP_SYS_NICE, SCHED_FIFO needs RLIMIT_RTPRIO), so it would usually just log EPERM.
- **The 1 MiB render pools (`BB_RENDER_POOLS`) aren't here.** bbhost's `engine/frame_pool.cpp` fixes the *borrow race* that leaked pool entries, not the pool size; I found no 256 KiB→1 MiB raise. It's the port's fix for the GXWorker write-through-null crash in a busy frame >1080p. Needs guest-site verification, so not a blind port.
- **SnormNz packed formats** — no `snorm_nz` anywhere in bbhost (`src/gcn/translate.*` handles snorm generally). Can't tell from the docs whether bbhost's table already covers the format shadPS4 was missing; would need that diff.
- Not worth chasing: the null/unbound descriptor-table crash (bbhost uses push descriptors and already reads "what no descriptor wrote" as zero, `render.cpp:10139`), and the "cleanup stops at its limits" perf item (bbhost's sweeps are already deadline-boxed).

Nothing else on that list is both absent and port-able without guessing at guest addresses.

// bbport (BB_DMEM_MB): the direct memory the game is told it has, in MiB. The
// stock 6 GiB (kDmemBaseSize); BB_DMEM_MB names another (the port's larger pool
// for a scene above 1080p is 9152 MiB), clamped to [kDmemBaseSize, kDmemMaxSize]
// - the same window hle_kernel_set_dmem_size() grows the pool in, so the switch
// only ever raises it. Below the stock size the game's own heaps no longer fit
// (which is why that function clamps there too), and the pool is fixed once the
// backing exists.
std::uint64_t g_dmem_size = [] {
    const char* e = std::getenv("BB_DMEM_MB");
    if (!e || !*e) return kDmemBaseSize;
    const std::uint64_t mib = std::strtoull(e, nullptr, 10);
    if (mib <= (kDmemBaseSize >> 20)) return kDmemBaseSize;
    if (mib >= (kDmemMaxSize >> 20)) return kDmemMaxSize;
    return mib << 20;
}();

Yes — and checking that turned up a bug I just fixed.

## Defaults in this branch (all **on**, unlike the Windows port where they're opt-in)

| Switch | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `BB_GC_RECENT_FRAMES` | 48 | Hang guard on |
| `BB_IMAGE_FREE_DELAY_FRAMES` | 32 | contributes to the same floor (`max` = 48) |
| `BB_VRAM_IDLE_SECONDS` | 30 | cold-texture sweep on (takes precedence over `BBHOST_VRAM_EVICT_S`) |
| `BB_VRAM_PRESSURE_PERCENT` | 85 | second sweep trigger on |
| `BB_DMEM_MB` | *unset* | no default — stock 6 GiB; only raises the pool when set |

Two caveats on "on":

- **The whole sweep needs a VRAM reserve.** `textures.cpp:3425` returns early unless `vram_reserve_bytes()` is nonzero — 512 MiB on a discrete GPU, none on an integrated one, tight memory, or `BBHOST_VRAM_RESERVE_MB=0`. So on an iGPU (Steam Deck included) neither the pressure nor the reserve trigger runs, and the hang guard is the only one of the three doing anything. `BBHOST_VRAM_EVICT_S=0` (exact string) is still the hard off.
- **A single `0` doesn't switch the hang guard off** — `max(48, 0)` is still 48. Both must be 0. Now documented in the comment.

## Fixed in this pass

`b063983` — **`BB_VRAM_PRESSURE_PERCENT=0` was inverted.** The Windows port documents `0` as off, but `used_pct >= 0` is always true, so `0` made the sweep evict up to 256 MiB of cold textures every second forever instead of never. Now gated on nonzero (`textures.cpp:3450`), and the sweep's comment states each switch's default, the `BB_VRAM_IDLE_SECONDS` precedence, and the shared floor.

**Verified:** diff read back; the gate is `budget && pressure_pct && used_pct >= pressure_pct`; working tree clean; four commits on `awakechan-fixes` (`81ed11c`, `e685767`, `b063983` on top of the original three). **Not run:** no build — Darwin host, bbhost targets Linux/Windows only, so these remain compiler-unverified.

**Remaining limitations**

  content: |
      # Building
      
      bbhost builds with CMake on x86-64 Linux. The Windows executable is
      cross-compiled from Linux with Clang and the mingw-w64 runtime; MSVC is not
      supported, because the host needs `__attribute__((sysv_abi))` to call into
      the game's code.
      
      ## Linux
      
      Requirements:
      
      - Clang or GCC with C++20, CMake 3.20+, Ninja or Make
      - libstdc++ 14 or newer
      - recent Vulkan headers (Ubuntu 24.04's 1.3.275 are too old; CI uses 1.4.350)
        and the Vulkan loader
      - zlib (required); libcurl, SDL3, ffmpeg (libavcodec, libavformat, libavutil,
        libswscale, libswresample) and SPIRV-Tools are optional but needed for a
        usable build: networking, windowing, audio, movies and shader optimisation
        are compiled out without them
      
      On Arch Linux the packages are `vulkan-headers vulkan-icd-loader sdl3 ffmpeg
      curl zlib spirv-tools`. On Ubuntu 24.04 the distribution's Vulkan headers and
      SDL are too old; `tools/ci_build.sh` builds them into a prefix and is the
      reference for a from-scratch build there.
      
      ```sh
      cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
      cmake --build build -j
      ```
      
      The result is `build/bbhost`, plus the official plugins in `build/plugins/`
      and the developer tools (`gcn2spv`, `gcndis`, `drawreplay`, ...).
      
      `-DBBHOST_RELEASE=ON` makes a release build, which by default checks at start
      whether a newer release is out and offers to open its page in the browser.
      
      ## Windows (cross-compiled)
      
      Requirements on the Linux machine: Clang, lld and llvm tools, the mingw-w64
      sysroot (`x86_64-w64-mingw32`), and wine for running the tests and the smoke
      run.
      
      ```sh
      tools/win_deps.sh       # once: zlib, SDL3, libcurl (schannel) and ffmpeg for the target
      cmake -S . -B build-win -G Ninja -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=cmake/mingw-toolchain.cmake \
            -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$PWD/build/win-deps/prefix -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
      cmake --build build-win
      ```
      
      The result is `build-win/bbhost.exe`, a single static executable that needs
      only the system DLLs and the GPU driver's `vulkan-1.dll`. It is linked at a
      fixed base (`0x600000000`) because the game's memory windows are reserved at
      fixed addresses before anything else runs.
      
      `tools/win_syntax_check.sh <file>` checks one source file for the Windows
      target while editing; `tools/win_tests.sh` builds and runs the low-level host
      tests (calling-convention thunks, TLS, `setjmp`/`longjmp`, `va_list`) under
      wine.
      
      ## Tests
      
      ```sh
      cd build && ctest --output-on-failure
      ```
      
      Tests that read game files skip unless `BBHOST_APP0` names the game folder
      (the one that contains `dvdroot_ps4`). No game file is ever part of the
      repository.
      
      `cmake --build build --target smoke` boots the game to the title screen and
      checks the log for crashes and unimplemented system calls; it needs a
      configured `bbhost.toml` with the game paths (see [running.md](running.md)).
      The Windows build has the same target under wine (`build-win`, target
      `smoke`).
      
      `build/gcn2spv --check <dvdroot_ps4>/shader/*.dcx` translates and validates
      every shader in the game's shader bundles.
      
      ## Packages
      
      | Target or script | Produces |
      |---|---|
      | `cmake --build build-win --target package-win` | `build/win/bbhost-win-<rev>.zip`, and the unstripped `.debug.exe` for symbolising crash reports |
      | `tools/package_linux.sh <bbhost> <outdir>` | a Linux tarball (built with `tools/linux_portable_build.sh` for a portable binary) |
      | `tools/package_steamdeck.sh` | the Linux package with the Steam Deck's settings |
      | `tools/package_plugins.sh` | the official plugins with their signatures |
      | `tools/package_playtest.sh` | tester kits for a playtest on a dev server, built by hand |
      
      The release workflow (`.github/workflows/release.yml`) builds the Windows,
      Linux and Steam Deck packages from a `v*` tag, signs `SHA256SUMS` and the
      official plugins with the release key, and publishes the release that bbhost's
      update check looks for. The bare executables it attaches are named the same in
      every release (`bbhost.exe`, and `bbhost` for Linux), so a shortcut or a Steam
      entry pointing at one keeps working when it is replaced. The packages pick no
      server, so they play on the live server (`https://thehuntersdream.com`),
      bbhost's default; `tools/check_release_bundle.sh` fails a release whose
      packages would go anywhere else, or that carries a playtest kit.
      
      ## Continuous integration
      
      `.github/workflows/build.yml` runs `tools/ci_build.sh` (a Linux build from
      scratch on Ubuntu 24.04, with the tests) and the Windows cross build on every
      push and pull request.

  content: |
      # Running bbhost
      
      ## What you need
      
      bbhost contains no game data. You bring:
      
      1. **The game files**: a dump of Bloodborne with the 1.09 update's files copied
         over it - the folder that contains `dvdroot_ps4`. Its
         `sce_sys/param.sfo` says `APP_VER 01.09`. The update can also stay in a
         folder of its own beside the game's, named after it with `-UPDATE` (or
         `-patch`) appended - `CUSA00900` and `CUSA00900-UPDATE`, the way shadPS4
         keeps a game library. bbhost then reads every file the update has from
         there and the rest from the game folder, as the console applies an update;
         the log names the folder (`FS update=`).
      2. **The 1.09 eboot**, decrypted to an ELF. Its SHA-256 must be
         `941f887a562aae054fac35af8cc8f27cf075f3d4cc2e029fb5ae2a663aaa5ae7`. Every
         patch, hook and engine layout in bbhost is an address in that build, so any
         other eboot stops at start with its hash and the version its dump reports.
         A dump without the update carries the 1.00 eboot, which will not do. When
         `paths.eboot` is not set, the game's own `eboot.bin` is used if it is
         decrypted already (a dump made for shadPS4), the update folder's first.
      
      Both must come from a copy of the game you own.
      
      And a PC with:
      
      - x86-64 Windows 10/11 or Linux
      - a GPU with a Vulkan 1.3 driver (recent NVIDIA, AMD or Intel; the Steam Deck works)
      - 16 GB of RAM and 8 GB of video memory are recommended; 6 GB NVIDIA cards
        play at 1080p too
      
      ## First run
      
      Started without a configuration, bbhost opens its setup window: pick the game
      folder and the eboot (both are checked as you go), choose the online server
      and account if you want to play online, and press Play. The window writes the
      per-user `bbhost.toml` and starts the game. `bbhost --setup` opens it again.
      
      Without a display (a headless run) bbhost writes a template config instead and
      tells you which paths to fill in.
      
      ## Configuration
      
      `bbhost.example.toml` lists every setting with its default. The configuration
      is read in layers, each overriding only the keys it sets:
      
      1. the per-user `bbhost.toml`: `%APPDATA%\bbhost` on Windows,
         `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/bbhost` or `~/.config/bbhost` on Linux
         (`BBHOST_CONFIG_DIR` replaces the folder);
      2. `bbhost.toml` in the working directory, or next to the executable;
      3. `--config <file>`;
      4. the command line: `--app0 <dir>`, `--data <dir>`, `--eboot <file>`, or the
         eboot as the last argument.
      
      The first log line names every file it read. Paths may use either slash; a
      relative path is taken from the folder of the file it is in.
      
      The in-game settings (F10, or the PC Settings, PC Graphics and Key Bindings
      entries the game's own System menu gains) are saved beside the per-user config
      in `bbhost-options.toml`.
      
      ## Saves
      
      Saves are in `<data>/saves/SPRJ0005`, where `<data>` defaults to
      `%LOCALAPPDATA%\bbhost\data` or `~/.local/share/bbhost/data`. Each time the
      game writes a save (at most every five minutes) a copy goes to
      `<data>/save-backups/`, and the newest eight are kept. To restore one, quit and
      copy its files over `<data>/saves/SPRJ0005`.
      
      The shader caches in `<data>/bbhost` (`translation-cache.bin`,
      `vulkan-pipeline-cache.bin`) belong to the shader translator that made them,
      which `shader-cache-build.txt` names. An update that leaves the translator
      alone keeps them, so it starts as fast as the build before it; one that
      changed the translator throws both away (`gpu: shader caches made by
      translator ..., this is translator ...: cleared`) and builds them again while
      the title and the loading screens are up, from `stage-manifest.bin`, the list
      of the game's shaders, which is kept. `BBHOST_KEEP_SHADER_CACHE=1` keeps them
      anyway. The files are safe to delete: the next start builds them again.
      
      ## Controls
      
      A controller works as on the console. Without one, the keyboard and mouse
      take over and the button prompts follow: the mouse turns the camera and works
      in the menus, and every action can be rebound (F10 or the game's Key Bindings
      menu) - to a key, any of five mouse buttons, or the wheel turned up or down
      (each notch a press). Hold Left Alt with the movement keys to walk, and two
      opposite keys held together cancel, both as in Dark Souls III. F9 opens the
      plugin menu and F10 bbhost's own settings.
      
      The mouse turns the camera the way Dark Souls III's PC version does: by an
      angle for each count the mouse reports, 0.25 degrees at the default
      sensitivity of 5 (0.1 at 0, 0.4 at 10), with no acceleration, no dead zone
      and no top speed, at any frame rate. The right stick turns it as on the
      console, and while the stick is moving the mouse waits. With a target locked
      on, a quick flick of the mouse switches targets. Mouse sensitivity and
      inverting either axis are on the game's PC Controls page; the game's own
      Camera settings are the stick's.
      
      With the mouse, the camera also stays where you put it: it does not turn by
      itself as the character moves - following the character round, or turning
      away from walls. Lock On with no target (Q) still swings it round behind the
      character. That follows the device you used last: pick up a controller and
      the game's own camera is back; touch the keyboard or mouse and it holds
      again. Mouse Auto-Rotation on the PC Camera page (F10: Mouse auto-rotation)
      turns it back on for the mouse too. It is the community's "Disable Camera
      Auto Rotation via Movement" patch made part of the camera - less its hold on
      the lock-on button's recentre; that patch, applied as before, still works as
      it always did, with any device.
      
      The character's name, a chalice glyph and the network password are typed in
      a box over the game, which stands in for the console's on-screen keyboard:
      Enter accepts, Escape cancels, Backspace deletes and Ctrl+V pastes. A
      controller's Cross (A) accepts and Circle (B) cancels. The boxes take what the
      console's keyboard offers - letters, digits and punctuation from plain ASCII -
      and a glyph takes its own 32 characters, lowercased as they are typed. The
      name box starts from `[player] name`, which the first key typed replaces;
      `[player] ime = "auto"` answers it with that name instead.
      
      ## Logs
      
      bbhost logs to standard error. The packages' `run-bbhost.bat` (Windows) and
      `run-bbhost.sh` (Linux) write each session's log to `logs/`. A bug report is
      most useful with that log attached.
      
      ## Troubleshooting
      
      **The eboot is refused.** It is not the 1.09 build. Use the update's
      `eboot.bin`, decrypted; the message says what the dump's `param.sfo` reports.
      
      **The game stops at start in `FileTransferTask.cpp(865)`, or the log says
      `patch: old-hunters skipped`.** The game folder holds files older than the
      1.09 update's: the update was never copied over it, or only its new files were
      (Windows' "Skip these files" when it asks about the ones already there). The
      log's `change appearance: off - not the 1.09 m21_00_00_00 layout` says the
      same. Copy the update's files over the game folder again, replacing the ones
      there, or keep the update in a `-UPDATE` folder beside it (above). Until The
      Old Hunters' own files are there, bbhost leaves the game as the edition
      without it: its title screen would otherwise be a flat green picture.
      
      **The graphics card stops responding.** When the GPU hangs and the system
      resets it, nothing can be drawn again in that session; bbhost stops the sound,
      says so in a box and exits. The next three starts run with the GPU's progress
      markers enabled, so the log of a second hang names the draw that hung - send
      that log. Overlays that hook Vulkan are a common cause: OBS's game capture is
      kept out automatically on AMD cards (`[video] obs_capture` changes that), and
      OBS's Window Capture records bbhost without any hook.
      
      **Wrong picture.** Wrong colours, a green or black screen, missing parts:
      press F12 in the game while it shows. bbhost writes that frame, every render
      target the last draws wrote and the draw list into a folder of its own beside
      the logs, `logs/f12-<date>-<time>/` (`build/` when there is no `logs/`
      folder, `BBHOST_CAPTURE_DIR` to choose), and the log names the folder. Zip it
      and send it with the log; `tools/f12_check.py <folder> <log>` checks it for
      the rendering bugs found so far. The images are PPM, which costs nothing to
      write; `BBHOST_F12_PNG=1` writes PNG instead, which any image viewer opens, a
      fifth of the size on disk, written over a few seconds in the background.
      `BBHOST_F12_TEXTURES=1` adds every texture the frame sampled, and the game
      pauses while it writes them.
      
      **Black or broken image in the world, or slow on a card with little video
      memory.** bbhost follows the driver's video memory budget as the game runs:
      it keeps the last 512 MiB for render targets, puts textures in system memory
      when the card is down to that, and moves them back once there is room. Every
      five seconds the log says `video memory: headroom ...`; look there, and for
      `video memory is full`, before anything else. Other programs holding video
      memory (browsers, OBS, a second game) shrink the budget. On a GPU with under
      7.5 GB free bbhost also holds less memory ahead (the log says `small video
      memory`). `BBHOST_VRAM_RESERVE_MB=0` goes back to placing everything until
      an allocation fails, `BBHOST_SMALL_VRAM=0` turns the small mode off.
      
      **AMD on Linux, no picture.** AMD's kernel driver only imports anonymous
      memory, so bbhost passes the game's memory to the GPU through `/dev/udmabuf`.
      If that device is not accessible to your user, the log says so; this udev rule
      fixes it:
      
      ```
      # /etc/udev/rules.d/70-udmabuf.rules
      KERNEL=="udmabuf", TAG+="uaccess"
      ```
      
      **AMD on Windows, slower in a window.** Play in fullscreen (Fullscreen in PC
      Settings, or Window mode in F10). In a window the desktop composites the
      picture, and AMD's driver then never completes the game's occlusion queries -
      the same as when the window is not focused - so the game, getting no answers,
      stops culling hidden geometry. On a Radeon 8060S at 1920x1080 that is 112 fps
      uncapped in a window against 161 in fullscreen, and at 60 fps the GPU 55% busy
      against 37%. The log's `occlusion:` line, every 300 flips, then says `0 dumps`
      or `left not ready (N queries unavailable)`.
      
      **Steam Deck.** Start bbhost from Steam (as a non-Steam game), in Game Mode or
      Desktop Mode; otherwise Steam's desktop controls send keys alongside the pad
      and every press acts twice. `tools/steamdeck/STEAMDECK.md` has the setup.
      
      ## Display and frame rate
      
      The picture keeps its aspect ratio, with ultrawide resolutions (21:9, 32:9)
      available in the settings. The resolution can be changed while playing.
      bbhost paces the game to the refresh rate of the display its window is on;
      `[video] vblank_hz` overrides a display that reports the wrong rate.
      
      The frame rate is the game's own speed, chosen when it starts (a change
      applies on the next run): 30 is the game as it shipped; 60, 90 and 120 run its
      logic at that rate; Uncapped steps it by the measured frame time (1/240 to 1/30
      s), at the display's refresh rate with V-Sync on and up to 240 fps with it off.
      Above 30 the game's step is the frame's measured time (at most 1/30 s), and the
      places that stepped a fixed 1/30 s a frame - physics, enemy AI, ragdolls,
      grass, the camera's easing, momentum, fades - follow it, so the game runs at
      the same speed at every rate (`engine/frame_rate.cpp`, from Kyo's FPS++ lists
      and yogesh1239's high-FPS fixes). The play time adds each frame's milliseconds
      with the fractions kept (the game drops them: its clock ran 4% slow at 60 and
      120). Above 60 and Uncapped the game paces itself
      and its frames are shown as they come, so 90 on a 60 Hz display shows 60 of
      them a second; a rate the machine cannot hold runs slower than real time in
      the few places that count frames.
      The follow camera runs the game's own values at every frame rate, converted
      to each frame's length, so above 30 it moves as it does at 30.
      `BBHOST_CAMERA_TUNING=fps++` runs Kyo's 60 FPS++ camera retune instead.
      `BBHOST_GAME_FPS=30|60|90|120|0` overrides the setting for a run (0 is
      uncapped), `BBHOST_UNCAPPED_FPS=N` sets the uncapped limit (30-240) whatever
      V-Sync says, and `BBHOST_FRAME_RATE_LOG=1` logs once a second the frame time the
      game steps by and values written from it. `BBHOST_TEST_FPS_SWING` (a test
      switch, at 60, 90, 120 or uncapped) moves the target while the game runs:
      `square:LO:HI:S` alternates LO and HI fps every S seconds, `random:LO:HI:S` picks
      a new rate in that range every S seconds, `jitter:LO:HI` every frame, and
      `sine:LO:HI:S` sweeps it - one process at two rates, or at one that never holds
      still, as a variable-refresh display or a busy scene makes it.
      `BBHOST_FIXED_TICK=<address>:<bytes>[,...]` (a test switch, same rates) runs
      a game function as a 30 Hz tick - once every other frame at 60, and so on, with
      the remainder carried - for logic that counts frames (`engine/frame_tick.h`). The start of the log says which rate
      runs and how many values and code sites were converted (`frame rate:` lines),
      and names any site whose bytes were not the expected ones (that rate is then
      refused: 90, 120 or uncapped falls back to 60).
      A frame goes to the screen as soon as the game has finished it; only its flip,
      which the game paces itself on, waits for the next tick of that clock. The game
      keeps two flips queued, and showing each frame at the tick that completed it
      held every frame two refreshes behind (`BBHOST_PRESENT_ON_ARRIVAL=0` brings that
      back, to compare). Every 300 flips the log's `pacing:` line says how late the
      clock's ticks woke and how long flips took from queued to shown and to
      completed.
      A flip completes - and what the frame used goes back to the game - only once
      the GPU has rendered that frame: on the console a flip is the GPU reaching it,
      and the game writes the next frames' data over what a completed frame read. A
      loading screen's flips, and those above 60 and Uncapped, do not wait for the
      clock, so they complete as soon as their frame has rendered; the log says how
      many of a loading screen's flips waited (`video: the loading screen's ...
      flips`). `BBHOST_FLIP_AFTER_GPU=0` completes a flip once the frame is recorded,
      as before: the game could then run several frames ahead of the GPU after a
      loading screen and overwrite what it had not read yet, which could hold the
      GPU for minutes.
      
      ## Online
      
      bbhost implements the PlayStation Network calls the game makes against a
      private server, so co-op, invasions, messages and bloodstains work between
      bbhost players. The setup window picks the server and links an account; see
      [online.md](online.md).
      
      ## The debug menu
      
      The developers' debug menu is still in the game, switched off. The **Debug
      Menu** plugin restores it (the community's "Restore Debug Menu" patch by
      Whitehawkx and auser1337): turn it on in the setup window's Plugins tab and
      start the game again. The `` ` `` key then opens and closes the menu (Key
      Bindings can move it). While it is open the character stands still; the arrows
      move, Enter opens an entry and Backspace goes back. Its text is in English; the
      plugin's **Menu text** setting brings back the developers' Japanese.
      
      The English is `plugins/debug_menu/strings_en.tsv`: each string's address in the
      1.09 eboot, a hash of the game's text there, and the English - no game text.
      `tools/debug_menu_strings.py list` shows the Japanese beside it from your own
      eboot, `missing` what has no English yet, and `check` tests every row (the
      hash, the printf conversions, the font). Corrections are welcome as pull
      requests. A few strings keep the developers' text because the game looks them
      up by name - the names the character scripts call the game's functions by, for
      one - and `check` refuses a row for any of them.
      
      The menu draws with a debug font the game does not ship. The plugin makes one
      from the public-domain X11 fonts k14 and 7x14, so nothing has to be
      downloaded. A `DbgFont14h.ccm` and `.tpf` of your own in the mods folder
      (`<mods>/dvdroot_ps4/adhoc/font/`; [modding.md](modding.md)) are used instead -
      `tools/build_debug_assets.sh` puts the community "Debug Menu Restoration"
      package's original font there.
      
      **Playing online:** the menu can hand out items and change the rules, so
      sessions with the plugin on keep their messages, bloodstains and statistics
      apart from other players'. Using it to cheat against other players - in their
      worlds, in invasions or on the leaderboards - gets an account banned. Trying it
      out online with friends is fine.

#!/bin/bash
# The continuous-integration build (.github/workflows/build.yml), and a
# from-scratch Linux build on a stock Ubuntu 24.04: the packages, the Vulkan
# headers (24.04's 1.3.275 are older than the renderer's), SDL3 and the movie
# decoders of ffmpeg built static into a prefix as tools/linux_portable_build.sh
# does, then bbhost, its tools and its tests, and ctest. No game files: the
# tests that read them skip (tests/test_app0.h).
#
#   tools/ci_build.sh                 everything, in build-ci/
#   CI_WORK=/somewhere tools/ci_build.sh
#   CI_APT=0                          the packages are already there
#   CI_CMAKE_ARGS="-DBBHOST_RELEASE=ON"   more configure arguments (a release build)
#   CI_PORTABLE=1                     link libstdc++ and libgcc statically, as
#                                     tools/linux_portable_build.sh does: the
#                                     binary tools/package_linux.sh packages
#
# The prefix (CI_WORK/prefix) is what the workflow caches between runs.
set -eu
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
SRC=$PWD
W=${CI_WORK:-$SRC/build-ci}
P=$W/prefix
VK_TAG=${VK_TAG:-v1.4.350}
SDL_TAG=${SDL_TAG:-release-3.4.16}
FFMPEG_VER=${FFMPEG_VER:-7.1.1}
JOBS=$(nproc)
# A prefix restored from a cache made in another directory (the repository's
# name is in the runner's path, and it can change) names
# that directory in its pkg-config files and CMake packages, and CMake refuses
# the paths that do not exist here. Such a prefix is built again.
if [ -f "$P/lib/pkgconfig/libavcodec.pc" ] && ! grep -q "^prefix=$P\$" "$P/lib/pkgconfig/libavcodec.pc"; then
    echo "the cached prefix was made in another directory ($(sed -n 's/^prefix=//p' "$P/lib/pkgconfig/libavcodec.pc")); building it again"
    rm -rf "$P"
fi
mkdir -p "$W/src" "$P"

if [ "${CI_APT:-1}" = 1 ]; then
    SUDO=$(command -v sudo || true)
    export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
    $SUDO apt-get update -q > "$W/apt-update.log" 2>&1

```

- path: /Users/sandvault-dn/bbwork/bbhost-nocrash/tools/ci_build.sh
  content: |
      #!/bin/bash
      # The continuous-integration build (.github/workflows/build.yml), and a
      # from-scratch Linux build on a stock Ubuntu 24.04: the packages, the Vulkan
      # headers (24.04's 1.3.275 are older than the renderer's), SDL3 and the movie
      # decoders of ffmpeg built static into a prefix as tools/linux_portable_build.sh
      # does, then bbhost, its tools and its tests, and ctest. No game files: the
      # tests that read them skip (tests/test_app0.h).
      #
      #   tools/ci_build.sh                 everything, in build-ci/
      #   CI_WORK=/somewhere tools/ci_build.sh
      #   CI_APT=0                          the packages are already there
      #   CI_CMAKE_ARGS="-DBBHOST_RELEASE=ON"   more configure arguments (a release build)
      #   CI_PORTABLE=1                     link libstdc++ and libgcc statically, as
      #                                     tools/linux_portable_build.sh does: the
      #                                     binary tools/package_linux.sh packages
      #
      # The prefix (CI_WORK/prefix) is what the workflow caches between runs.
      set -eu
      cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
      SRC=$PWD
      W=${CI_WORK:-$SRC/build-ci}
      P=$W/prefix
      VK_TAG=${VK_TAG:-v1.4.350}
      SDL_TAG=${SDL_TAG:-release-3.4.16}
      FFMPEG_VER=${FFMPEG_VER:-7.1.1}
      JOBS=$(nproc)
      # A prefix restored from a cache made in another directory (the repository's
      # name is in the runner's path, and it can change) names
      # that directory in its pkg-config files and CMake packages, and CMake refuses
      # the paths that do not exist here. Such a prefix is built again.
      if [ -f "$P/lib/pkgconfig/libavcodec.pc" ] && ! grep -q "^prefix=$P\$" "$P/lib/pkgconfig/libavcodec.pc"; then
          echo "the cached prefix was made in another directory ($(sed -n 's/^prefix=//p' "$P/lib/pkgconfig/libavcodec.pc")); building it again"
          rm -rf "$P"
      fi
      mkdir -p "$W/src" "$P"
      
      if [ "${CI_APT:-1}" = 1 ]; then
          SUDO=$(command -v sudo || true)
          export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
          $SUDO apt-get update -q > "$W/apt-update.log" 2>&1
          $SUDO apt-get install -y -q --no-install-recommends clang lld llvm cmake ninja-build pkg-config make nasm curl \
              git libstdc++-14-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev libvulkan-dev zlib1g-dev spirv-tools python3 xz-utils \
              ca-certificates libx11-dev libxext-dev libxrandr-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libxfixes-dev libxss-dev \
              libxtst-dev libxkbcommon-dev libwayland-dev wayland-protocols libegl-dev libdecor-0-dev libpulse-dev \
              libasound2-dev libpipewire-0.3-dev libdbus-1-dev libudev-dev libdrm-dev libgbm-dev \
              > "$W/apt-install.log" 2>&1 || { tail -20 "$W/apt-install.log"; exit 1; }
      fi
      # libstdc++ 14: the HLE libc calls std::acosf and friends, which 13 lacks.
      export CC=clang CXX=clang++
      
      fetch() {  # fetch NAME URL DIR-GLOB
          if ! ls -d "$W/src"/$3 > /dev/null 2>&1; then
              echo "fetching $1"
              curl -sSL -m 600 -o "$W/src/$1.tar" "$2"
              tar xf "$W/src/$1.tar" -C "$W/src" --no-same-owner
              rm -f "$W/src/$1.tar"
          fi
      }
      
      # Vulkan headers, newer than the distribution's.
      if [ ! -f "$P/include/vulkan/vulkan_core.h" ]; then
          fetch vulkan-headers "https://github.com/KhronosGroup/Vulkan-Headers/archive/refs/tags/$VK_TAG.tar.gz" 'Vulkan-Headers-*'
          v=$(ls -d "$W"/src/Vulkan-Headers-* | head -1)
          cmake -S "$v" -B "$W/vk-headers" -G Ninja -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$P" > "$W/vk-headers.log"
          cmake --install "$W/vk-headers" > /dev/null
      fi
      
      # SDL3, static (its window and audio backends are loaded at run time).
      if [ ! -f "$P/lib/libSDL3.a" ]; then
          fetch sdl3 "https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL/archive/refs/tags/$SDL_TAG.tar.gz" 'SDL-*'
          s=$(ls -d "$W"/src/SDL-* | head -1)
          cmake -S "$s" -B "$W/sdl3" -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$P" \
              -DCMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR=lib -DSDL_SHARED=OFF -DSDL_STATIC=ON -DSDL_TEST_LIBRARY=OFF -DSDL_TESTS=OFF \
              -DSDL_EXAMPLES=OFF -DCMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE=ON > "$W/sdl3-configure.log"
          cmake --build "$W/sdl3" > "$W/sdl3-build.log"
          cmake --install "$W/sdl3" > /dev/null
      fi
      
      # ffmpeg, only the movie decoders (tools/win_deps.sh has the reasons), static.
      if [ ! -f "$P/lib/libavcodec.a" ]; then

              --enable-pic --disable-programs --disable-doc --disable-network --disable-everything \
              --enable-decoder=h264,hevc,aac,mp3 --enable-demuxer=mov,mp3,aac --enable-parser=h264,hevc,aac \

              > "$W/ffmpeg-configure.log" 2>&1 \

              || { tail -20 "$W/ffmpeg-configure.log" "$W/ffmpeg-build.log"; exit 1; }

      fi

      export PKG_CONFIG_PATH=$P/lib/pkgconfig
      static=""
      [ "${CI_PORTABLE:-0}" = 1 ] && static="-static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc"
      cmake -S "$SRC" -B "$W/build" -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$P" \
          -DVulkan_INCLUDE_DIR="$P/include" -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS="$static -fuse-ld=lld" \
          -DCMAKE_MODULE_LINKER_FLAGS="${static#-static-libstdc++ } -fuse-ld=lld" ${CI_CMAKE_ARGS:-} > "$W/bbhost-configure.log" \
          || { tail -30 "$W/bbhost-configure.log"; exit 1; }
      grep -E "^-- bbhost" "$W/bbhost-configure.log" || true
      cmake --build "$W/build" -j"$JOBS" 2>&1 | tee "$W/bbhost-build.log" | grep -E "error|warning: unused|FAILED" | head -40 || true
      [ "${PIPESTATUS[0]}" = 0 ] || { echo "build failed (log: $W/bbhost-build.log)"; exit 1; }
      (cd "$W/build" && ctest --output-on-failure)
      echo "ci build: $W/build/bbhost"
      
  referencedBy: {}

Here's what CI itself installs, and the headers answer.

## apt (the "most of the requirements" list, verbatim from `tools/ci_build.sh:41`)

```sh
sudo apt-get update
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    clang lld llvm cmake ninja-build pkg-config make nasm curl \
    git libstdc++-14-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev libvulkan-dev zlib1g-dev spirv-tools python3 xz-utils \
    ca-certificates libx11-dev libxext-dev libxrandr-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libxfixes-dev libxss-dev \
    libxtst-dev libxkbcommon-dev libwayland-dev wayland-protocols libegl-dev libdecor-0-dev \
    libpulse-dev libasound2-dev libpipewire-0.3-dev libdbus-1-dev libudev-dev libdrm-dev libgbm-dev
```

Roughly: toolchain (`clang lld llvm cmake ninja-build`), `libstdc++-14-dev` (the HLE libc calls `std::acosf`; 13 lacks it), `libvulkan-dev` for the loader, `zlib1g-dev`, `spirv-tools`, and then the X11/Wayland/audio/GBM dev packages — those last two lines are what a **static SDL3 build** needs, not bbhost itself.

## Vulkan headers

Ubuntu 24.04's `libvulkan-dev` is **1.3.275** (loader *and* headers) and its headers are too old for the renderer. CI pulls them from **KhronosGroup/Vulkan-Headers** at tag `v1.4.350` and installs them into a prefix:

```sh
PREFIX=$HOME/bbprefix              # same idea as build-ci/prefix
mkdir -p "$PREFIX" && cd /tmp && rm -rf vk-headers && mkdir vk-headers && cd vk-headers
curl -sSL -o vk.tar.gz \
  https://github.com/KhronosGroup/Vulkan-Headers/archive/refs/tags/v1.4.350.tar.gz
tar xf vk.tar.gz
cmake -S Vulkan-Headers-1.4.350 -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$PREFIX"
cmake --install build
```

Then, and this is the part that matters, point CMake at them:

```sh
-DVulkan_INCLUDE_DIR="$PREFIX/include"
```

CMakeLists uses `find_package(Vulkan QUIET)` and links `Vulkan::Headers` + `Vulkan::Vulkan` (`CMakeLists.txt:261-269`), so the **loader stays the distro's** `libvulkan.so` — you only replace the headers. That exact combination (prefix headers, `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libvulkan.so`) is what CI builds with, so it's a known-good pairing; bbhost targets a Vulkan 1.3 driver anyway, 1.4 headers are just newer than needed.

Alternative if you'd rather not build them: the LunarG Vulkan SDK tarball (`vulkan.lunarg.com`) ships current headers + loader, but grafting the distro loader onto it is what CI avoids.

## One gap apt can't fill: SDL3

`libsdl3-dev` **does not exist in 24.04** — it only landed in 25.10 (there's a `noble-bleed` PPA carrying 3.2.26). CI builds SDL3 `release-3.4.16` from source, statically:

```sh
curl -sSL -o sdl3.tar.gz https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL/archive/refs/tags/release-3.4.16.tar.gz
tar xf sdl3.tar.gz
cmake -S SDL-release-3.4.16 -B build-sdl3 -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$PREFIX" -DCMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR=lib \
      -DSDL_SHARED=OFF -DSDL_STATIC=ON -DSDL_TEST_LIBRARY=OFF -DSDL_TESTS=OFF \
      -DSDL_EXAMPLES=OFF -DCMAKE_POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE=ON
cmake --build build-sdl3 && cmake --install build-sdl3
```

Without it you get a build, but a headless-only one — `CMakeLists.txt:313` prints `bbhost: SDL3/Vulkan not found; headless only`, no window or audio.

## Honest recommendation

All of the above is `tools/ci_build.sh` with `CI_APT` unset. If you want to keep your own prefix and flags:

```sh
CI_APT=0 CI_WORK=$HOME/bbwork tools/ci_build.sh   # skips apt, still builds the deps into the prefix
```

`VK_TAG`, `SDL_TAG` and `FFMPEG_VER` are overridable at the top of the script if you want a newer header tag than CI's pin.

      #!/bin/bash
      # Packs a Linux build into the tarball another Linux machine runs from, the
      # counterpart of tools/win_package.sh: the binary without its DWARF, the patch
      # manifests it applies (patches/, looked for next to the binary), the plugin
      # header, the example config, a README with what the machine must have, a
      # launcher that keeps a log file, and the empty data/, logs/ and build/ (frame
      # dumps) the run writes into: the release's Linux bundle. Nothing in it picks
      # a server: bbhost's defaults are the live server's (https://thehuntersdream.com).
      # The unstripped binary is kept beside the tarball under the same revision
      # name, for symbolizing a crash report from that machine.
      #   tools/package_linux.sh [BIN] [OUTDIR]
      # BIN defaults to build-linux-portable/build/bbhost (tools/linux_portable_build.sh),
      # the build that runs on other distributions; build/bbhost only runs on a
      # machine as new as this one. Never packs game files (eboot, dump, keys).
      set -eu
      cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
      bin=${1:-build-linux-portable/build/bbhost}
      out=${2:-build/linux}
      [ -x "$bin" ] || { echo "no binary at $bin (tools/linux_portable_build.sh builds it)"; exit 1; }
      rev=$(git -c core.excludesFile=/dev/null rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
      # A release (HEAD at a v* tag) is named for its version, anything else for its revision.
      if tag=$(git -c core.excludesFile=/dev/null describe --tags --exact-match --match 'v[0-9]*' 2>/dev/null); then
          rev=$tag
      fi
      if [ -n "$(git -c core.excludesFile=/dev/null status --porcelain --untracked-files=no 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
          rev="$rev+"
      fi
      name=bbhost-linux-$rev
      dir=$out/$name
      rm -rf "$dir"
      mkdir -p "$dir/data" "$dir/logs" "$dir/plugins" "$dir/build"
      cp -r patches "$dir/patches"
      cp include/bbhost_plugin.h "$dir/plugins/"
      cp LICENSE "$dir/LICENSE"
      tools/package_plugins.sh "$(dirname "$bin")/plugins" "$dir/plugins"
      objcopy --strip-debug "$bin" "$dir/bbhost" 2>/dev/null || llvm-objcopy --strip-debug "$bin" "$dir/bbhost"
      chmod +x "$dir/bbhost"
      cp "$bin" "$out/$name.debug"
      cp bbhost.example.toml "$dir/bbhost.example.toml"
      
      # What the binary still loads from the system, from its own dynamic section,
      # so the README cannot drift from the build.
      needed=$(readelf -d "$bin" | sed -n 's/.*Shared library: \[\(.*\)\]/\1/p' | tr '\n' ' ')

      glibcxx=$(objdump -T "$bin" | grep -o 'GLIBCXX_[0-9.]*' | sort -uV | tail -1)
